summary: Defines i;unicode-casemap, a simple way to compare Unicode strings without caring about upper or lower case. It provides rules for equality, substring matching and ordering, so protocols that need to sort or search text can agree on one comparison. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine sorting a pile of name tags where it does not matter if someone wrote JOHN or john. This gives computers one shared rule for treating big and small letters as the same when comparing words.

questions: how to compare unicode strings case-insensitively
how does case insensitive unicode comparison work
subtitle: A simple, case-insensitive way to compare Unicode text for equality, ordering and substring matching.

tldr.problem: The older i;ascii-casemap collation only handles the 26 Latin letters, so it gives poor results for text with non-ASCII characters.
tldr.mechanism: Each string is converted to Unicode, titlecased and decomposed (a subset of Normalization Form KD), written out as UTF-8, and then compared byte by byte with i;octet.
tldr.outcome: It is meant as an alternative to, and preferred over, i;ascii-casemap, but it is not locale sensitive and is often a poor fit for natural-language sorting.

today: RFC 5051 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Unicode Casemap Collation
sections.content:
A collation is a named set of rules for comparing strings. The i;ascii-casemap collation is simple to implement and ignores case for the 26 Latin letters. It is used as the default or baseline comparator in some application protocols.

It does not give satisfactory results for non-ASCII characters. i;unicode-casemap extends the idea: it ignores case for many more characters and also collates characters with diacriticals together with their plain forms. The RFC says it is intended to be an alternative to, and preferred over, i;ascii-casemap. It does not replace the i;basic collation.
sections.plainLanguage: An old rule only knew how to treat big and small English letters as twins. This new rule knows many more letters, and it even treats a letter with a little hat or dots on top as the same as the plain one.

sections.title: Preparing a String for Comparison
sections.content:
The collation provides equality, substring and ordering operations. Its validity test returns 'valid' for any input. Before any comparison, each input string is turned into a titlecased canonicalized UTF-8 string, using UnicodeData.txt.

  • Step 1: read a sequence in the string's charset, check that it is valid, and convert it to a Unicode codepoint. UTF-8 input must be valid UTF-8, so overlong sequences are invalid.
  • Step 2a: if the codepoint has a titlecase property, which is normally the same as uppercase, replace it with that.
  • Step 2b: if the result has a decomposition property of any type, replace it with the decomposition, and repeat until nothing more decomposes. The RFC says this is effectively Normalization Form KD.
  • Step 3: append the resulting codepoints in UTF-8 form to the prepared string.
  • Step 4: repeat until the input is used up.

After both strings are prepared, equality, ordering and substring operations work as for i;octet, which is a plain octet-by-octet comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: First every word is rewritten in one standard form: all letters made capital and fancy letters broken into plain letter plus little mark. Then the two rewritten words are compared piece by piece.

sections.title: A Worked Example and Fallback Rules
sections.content:
The RFC's example is codepoint U+01C4 (LATIN CAPITAL LETTER DZ WITH CARON). Its titlecase is U+01C5, which decomposes to U+0044 and U+017E. Then U+017E decomposes to U+007A and U+030C (COMBINING CARON). None of those three has a further decomposition, so U+01C4 becomes U+0044 U+007A U+030C.

Strings may be in arbitrary and mixed character sets, as long as each string's charset is identified and it can be converted to Unicode. If the charset is unknown, or an invalid sequence appears, conversion stops, partial results are thrown away, and the original string is compared unchanged with i;octet. Such strings are not rejected, they are treated as binary.
sections.plainLanguage: If the computer cannot read a word's alphabet at all, it does not give up. It just compares the raw letters exactly as they are.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
An implementation may use a different preparation process if it produces the same results. For example, it can convert every string to UTF-16 or UTF-32 before the step 2 actions, or use UTF-32 instead of UTF-8 in step 3 when all input strings are or can be converted to Unicode.

UTF-16 is not suitable as the form used in step 3. Its surrogates would make i;octet collate codepoints U+E0000 through U+FFFF after non-BMP codepoints.

The collation is not locale sensitive. Functions such as strcasecmp and toupper are sometimes locale sensitive and may inconsistently casemap letters, so take care when using OS-supplied functions to implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: You may follow a different recipe if the cake comes out exactly the same. But do not use a recipe that changes depending on which country your oven is in.

sections.title: Where It Works and Where It Does Not
sections.content:
The collation is well suited to use with many Internet protocols and computer languages. Use with natural language is often inappropriate. Even though it apparently supports languages such as Swahili and English, in real-world use it tends to mis-sort several kinds of string.

  • People and place names containing scripts that are not collated according to alphabetical order.
  • Words with diacriticals. It generally does better than i;ascii-casemap for most but not all languages: German umlaut letters sort correctly, but some Scandinavian letters do not.
  • Names such as 'Lloyd', which in Welsh sorts after 'Lyon', unlike in English.
  • Strings with other symbols, such as euro and pound sterling signs, quotation marks other than the plain double quote, and dashes or hyphens.
sections.plainLanguage: It is great for computer jobs like looking up a mailbox name. It is not so great for sorting a phone book in every language, because every language has its own ideas about ABC order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of UTF-8, stringprep and the Unicode security report apply and are normative. Results vary by implementation, and implementations MUST consider whether that matters for their use case.

  • New Unicode characters may have decomposition or titlecase properties that an implementation built on an older Unicode revision does not know.
  • An implementation MAY use an NFKD library routine that also normalizes out-of-order diacriticals, which matters only for ill-formed UTF-8 input.
  • The set of charsets in step 1 is open-ended. UTF-8, and by extension US-ASCII, are the only mandatory-to-implement charsets. Implementations SHOULD support as many likely charsets as feasible, to avoid poor collation from the fall-through to binary comparison.
  • Other charsets may gain new characters over time.

An attacker may craft ill-formed input or input in an unknown charset to affect the result. Even well-formed input can cause surprises: substituting U+0391 (Greek capital alpha) or U+0410 (Cyrillic capital A) for U+0041 can prevent a match between strings that look the same.
sections.plainLanguage: Tricksters can swap a letter for a look-alike from another alphabet. The two words look the same to you, but the computer sees them as different.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content: The collation is registered in the collation registry defined in RFC 4790. The registration gives the identifier i;unicode-casemap, the title 'Unicode Casemap', global scope, common intended use, and the operations equality, order and substring. The owner is the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: It was written into an official list of comparison rules, with its name and what it can do.

data.title: Preparing U+01C4
data.code:
U+01C4  LATIN CAPITAL LETTER DZ WITH CARON
  titlecase       -> U+01C5
  decomposition   -> U+0044 U+017E
  decomposition   -> U+0044 U+007A U+030C
